en: Majjhima Nikāya 97,
the Dhanañjāni Sutta:
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was wandering on tour among the Southern Hills together with a large community of monks.

Then a certain monk who had completed the rains residence at Rājagaha went to the Venerable Sāriputta in the Southern Hills; having approached him, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. As the bhikkhu was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said to him:
"I hope, friend, that the Blessed One is free from illness and strong?
"The Blessed One is indeed free from illness, friend, and he is strong," he replied.
“But, friend, is the community of monks healthy and strong?
“The community of monks, friend, is indeed healthy and strong.
“In this place, friend, there is a brahmin named Dhanañjāni at the rice-heap gate.”
“Is the brahmin Dhanañjāni healthy and strong, friend?
“The brahmin Dhanañjāni is indeed healthy and strong, friend.
“But is the brahmin Dhanañjāni diligent, friend?”
“But how, friends, can there be heedfulness for the brahmin Dhanañjāni?
Friends, the brahmin Dhanañjāni, relying on the king, plunders the brahmin householders; relying on the brahmin householders, he plunders the king.
Even his wife, who was brought from a faithful family and possessed of faith, has passed away.”
“His other wife is faithless, brought from a family lacking faith.
“We have indeed heard what was ill-spoken, friends; we have indeed heard what was ill-spoken, friends—that we should have heard Dhanañjāni the brahmin while he was negligent!”
"Perhaps we might at some time or other meet with the brahmin Dhanañjāni; perhaps there might be some conversation between us.
Then, having stayed in Dakkhiṇāgiri for as long as he pleased, the Venerable Sāriputta set out on a wandering tour toward Rājagaha.
Traveling by stages on his tour, he eventually arrived at Rājagaha.
At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Sāriputta dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms.
Now at that time, the brahmin Dhanañjāni was having cows milked in a cow-pen outside the city.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta, having walked for alms in Rājagaha and returned from his almsround after his meal, approached the brahmin Dhanañjāni.
The brahmin Dhanañjāni saw the Venerable Sāriputta coming from afar.
Having seen him, he approached the Venerable Sāriputta and, having approached, said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“From here, Master Sāriputta, is milk; let it be drunk first, for it will then be time for the meal.
“Enough, brahmin.
My meal-duty is finished today.”
“I shall have my midday rest at the foot of such-and-such a tree;
you should come there.
“Very well, sir,” the brahmin Dhanañjāni replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
Then, after his meal and having finished his breakfast, the brahmin Dhanañjāni approached the Venerable Sāriputta. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. As the brahmin Dhanañjāni was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to him:
"I hope, Dhanañjāni, that you are being diligent?"
“Master Sāriputta, from where could diligence come for us, who must support our mother and father,
support our children and wife, support our slaves and laborers, perform duties toward friends and companions, perform duties toward kinsmen and blood relations,
perform duties toward guests, and [perform duties] toward deceased ancestors?
"Should one perform what is to be done for deceased ancestors, perform what is to be done for deities, perform what is to be done for kings,
and also nourish and develop this body?
"What do you think, Dhanañjāni?"

In this case, someone might, for the sake of his mother and father, act unrighteously and live an immoral life. On account of that unrighteous and immoral conduct, the wardens of hell might drag him away to hell.
Would he be able to say, "I acted unrighteously and lived an immoral life for the sake of my mother and father;
do not let the wardens of hell take me"? Or would his mother and father be able to say, "He acted unrighteously... [for our sake]..."?
“‘He has been one who conducts himself unevenly; do not let him fall into hell, O guardians of hell!’?
“Certainly not, Master Sāriputta.
On the contrary, while he is still crying out, the guardians of hell would throw him into hell.”
“What do you think, Dhanañjāni?

Suppose here someone, for the sake of his wife and children, were to act unrighteously and immorally. Because of that practice of unrighteousness and immorality, the wardens of hell might drag him off to hell.
Would he be able to say: ‘I acted unrighteously and immorally for the sake of my wife and children; let [the suffering] not [be mine]’?”
“Would his wife and children say, ‘He was a practitioner of unrighteousness and of immoral conduct;
let not the wardens of hell take him to hell’?
“Certainly not, Master Sāriputta.”
“Then, while he is still crying out, the wardens of hell would throw him into hell.

“What do you think, Dhanañjāni? Suppose here someone were to act unrighteously and improperly for the sake of a slave, laborer, or servant; would the wardens of hell drag that person to hell on account of that unrighteous and improper conduct?
“Would he be able to say: ‘I indeed acted unrighteously and improperly for the sake of a slave, laborer, or servant’?”

“Would the wardens of hell say, ‘Do not let him go to hell,’ or would his slaves, laborers, or servants say, ‘This man was indeed unrighteous and immoral in his conduct; do not let him go to hell, wardens of hell’?
“Certainly not, Master Sāriputta.”
“Then, while he is still crying out, the wardens of hell would throw him into hell.

“What do you think, Dhanañjāni? Suppose here someone, for the sake of friends and companions, were to act unrighteously and improperly; and because of that unrighteous and improper conduct, the wardens of hell were to drag him toward hell.
Would he be able to say: ‘I indeed acted unrighteously and improperly for the sake of friends and companions; let me not [suffer]...’?”
“Would the wardens of hell say, ‘This man belongs to us, he was one who practiced unrighteousness and lived crookedly;
do not let him go to hell,’ or would his friends and companions say, ‘He was indeed our cause for practicing unrighteousness and living crookedly; do not let him go to hell, wardens of hell’?
“Certainly not, Master Sāriputta.”
Then, while he was still crying out, the wardens of hell would throw him into hell.

What do you think, Dhanañjāni? Suppose here someone, for the sake of his kinsmen and blood relations, were to act unrighteously and improperly; would the wardens of hell drag that person into hell on account of his unrighteous and improper conduct?
Would he be able to say: ‘I indeed acted unrighteously and improperly for the sake of my kinsmen and blood relations’?”

“‘O guardians of hell, do not let me go to hell! Or would his kinsmen and blood relatives be able to say, ‘He was indeed one who acted unrighteously and improperly on our account; do not let him go to hell, O guardians of hell’?
“Certainly not, Master Sāriputta.”
“Then, even as he is still crying out, the wardens of hell would cast him into hell.

“What do you think, Dhanañjāni? Suppose here someone, for the sake of guests, were to act unrighteously and immorally; would the wardens of hell drag that person to hell on account of his unrighteous and immoral conduct?
Would he be able to say: ‘I indeed acted unrighteously and immorally for the sake of guests; let not...’?”
‘The hell-dwellers [are coming] for hell!’; or would his guests receive him, saying, ‘This man was indeed one who practiced unrighteousness and lived crookedly on our account;
do not let the hell-dwellers take him to hell’?
“Certainly not, Master Sāriputta.”
Then, while he is still crying out, the wardens of hell would throw him into hell.

What do you think, Dhanañjāni? Suppose here someone, for the sake of his deceased ancestors, were to act unrighteously and immorally; would the wardens of hell drag that person into hell on account of that unrighteous and immoral conduct?
Would he be able to say: ‘I indeed acted unrighteously and immorally for the sake of my deceased ancestors; let them [the ancestors] share this suffering with me’?”
“‘Do not let the wardens of hell take me to hell,’ or would his departed ancestors obtain this: ‘He was indeed one who practiced unrighteousness and lived contrary to the Dhamma for our sake;
do not let the wardens of hell take him to hell’?
“Certainly not, Master Sāriputta.”
“Then, while he is still crying out, the wardens of hell would throw him into hell.

“What do you think, Dhanañjāni? Suppose here someone were to act unrighteously and immorally for the sake of the deities; because of that practice of unrighteousness and immorality, the wardens of hell would drag him toward hell.
Would he be able to say: ‘I indeed acted unrighteously and immorally for the sake of the deities; do not [drag] me...’?”
“‘Hell, hell-guardians! Or would deities perhaps say to him, ‘This man was indeed a practitioner of unrighteousness and of uneven conduct because of us;
do not let him go to hell, O hell-guardians’?
“Certainly not, Master Sāriputta.”
Then, while he is still crying out, the wardens of hell would throw him into hell.

What do you think, Dhanañjāni? Suppose here someone were unrighteous and unjust in his conduct for the sake of a king; because of that unrighteous and unjust conduct, the wardens of hell would drag him toward hell.
Would he be able to say: ‘I was indeed unrighteous and unjust in my conduct for the sake of a king; do not lead me to hell’?”
"Or would a king obtain [the authority] over the hell-wardens, saying: 'This man was indeed one who acted unrighteously and improperly on our account;
do not let him go to hell, O hell-wardens'?
"Certainly not, sir Sāriputta."
Then, while he was still crying out, the wardens of hell would throw him into hell.

What do you think, Dhanañjāni? Suppose here someone, for the sake of nourishing and strengthening his body, were to live unrighteously and immorally; would the wardens of hell drag that person to hell on account of his unrighteous and immoral conduct?
Would he be able to say: ‘I indeed lived unrighteously and immorally for the sake of nourishing and strengthening my body’?”

‘He was one who acted contrary to the Dhamma and lived unrighteously for the sake of nourishing and fattening his body; do not let the wardens of hell cast him into hell,’ or if others were to say of him:
‘This man indeed acted contrary to the Dhamma and lived unrighteously for the sake of nourishing and fattening his body; do not let the wardens of hell cast him into hell’?
“Certainly not, Master Sāriputta.”
“Then, even as he is screaming, the wardens of hell would cast him into hell.

“What do you think, Dhanañjāni: between one who, for the sake of his mother and father, would act unrighteously and improperly, and one who, for the sake of his mother and father, would act righteously and properly—which of these is better?”
“Master Sāriputta, for one who, for the sake of mother and father, would be unrighteous and immoral, that would not be better;
but rather, Master Sāriputta, for one who, for the sake of mother and father, would be righteous and moral—that alone would be better here.
For unrighteousness and immorality, Master Sāriputta, righteousness and morality are better.”
“There are, Dhanañjāni, other righteous occupations with a cause by which one can support one’s mother and father, without committing evil deeds and while practicing the way of merit.

What do you think, Dhanañjāni: would it be better for one to act unrighteously and immorally for the sake of one’s wife and children, or to act righteously and morally for the sake of one’s wife and children?”
“Indeed, Master Sāriputta, for one who would act unrighteously and improperly for the sake of wife and children, that is not good;
but for one who would act righteously and properly for the sake of wife and children, that alone is better in this case.
For, Master Sāriputta, acting righteously and properly is better than acting unrighteously and improperly.”
“There are, Dhanañjāni, other righteous occupations with a cause by which one can support one’s wife and children, without committing evil deeds and while practicing the way of merit.

What do you think, Dhanañjāni: would it be better for one to act unrighteously and immorally for the sake of slaves, laborers, and servants, or to act righteously and morally for the sake of slaves, laborers, and servants?”
“Master Sāriputta, for one who would act unrighteously and improperly for the sake of a slave, laborer, or servant, that is not better;
whereas, Master Sāriputta, for one who would act righteously and properly for the sake of a slave, laborer, or servant, that alone is better here.
Between acting unrighteously and improperly and acting righteously and properly, Master Sāriputta, acting righteously and properly is better.”

“Dhanañjāni, there are indeed other righteous occupations that have their own causes, by which one can support slaves, laborers, and servants, yet commit no evil deed and instead practice the path of merit.

What do you think, Dhanañjāni: between one who, for the sake of friends and companions, would act unrighteously and improperly, and one who, for the sake of friends and companions, would act righteously and properly—which is better?”
“Indeed, Master Sāriputta, for one who would act unrighteously and improperly for the sake of friends and companions, that is not better;
but rather, Master Sāriputta, for one who would act righteously and properly for the sake of friends and companions, that alone is better here.
Between acting unrighteously and improperly and acting righteously and properly, Master Sāriputta, acting righteously and properly is better.”

“There are, Dhanañjāni, other righteous occupations that have a cause, by which one can perform what is to be done for friends and companions, without committing evil deeds, and instead practicing the way of merit.

What do you think, Dhanañjāni: between one who, for the sake of relatives and kin, would act unrighteously and improperly, and one who, for the sake of relatives and kin, would act righteously and properly—which of these is better?”
“Master Sāriputta, for one who would act unrighteously and improperly for the sake of kinsmen and blood relations, that is not better;
but rather, Master Sāriputta, for one who would act righteously and properly for the sake of kinsmen and blood relations, that alone is better here.
For unrighteous conduct and improper conduct, Master Sāriputta, righteous conduct and proper conduct are better.”

“There are, Dhanañjāni, other righteous occupations that have a cause, by which one can perform what is to be done for one’s kinsmen and blood relations, without committing evil deeds and instead following a path of merit.

What do you think, Dhanañjāni: between one who, for the sake of guests, would act unrighteously and immorally, and one who, for the sake of guests, would act righteously and morally—of these two, which is better?”
“Master Sāriputta, for one who would act unrighteously and immorally for the sake of guests, that is not better;
but for one who would act righteously and morally for the sake of guests, that alone is better here.
Master Sāriputta, compared to unrighteous conduct and immoral conduct, righteous conduct and moral conduct are better.”
“There are, Dhanañjāni, other righteous occupations that have their own causes, by which one can perform the duties toward guests, commit no evil deed, and practice the way of merit.

What do you think, Dhanañjāni: between one who, for the sake of the deceased ancestors, would act unrighteously and improperly, and one who, for the sake of the deceased ancestors, would act righteously and properly—which of these is better?”
“Master Sāriputta, for one who, for the sake of the deceased ancestors, would live unrighteously and immorally, that is not better;
but for one who, Master Sāriputta, for the sake of the deceased ancestors, would live righteously and morally, that alone is better here.
Between unrighteous conduct and immoral conduct, Master Sāriputta, righteous conduct and moral conduct are better.”

“There are, Dhanañjāni, other righteous occupations based on causes by which one can perform the duties toward one’s deceased ancestors, without committing evil deeds and instead following a path of merit.

What do you think, Dhanañjāni: between one who, for the sake of the deities, would act unrighteously and improperly, and one who, for the sake of the deities, would act righteously and properly—which of these is better?”
“Master Sāriputta, for one who would act unrighteously and improperly for the sake of the deities, that would not be good;
but for one who would act righteously and properly for the sake of the deities, that alone is better here.
Master Sāriputta, acting righteously and properly is better than acting unrighteously and improperly.”
“There are, Dhanañjāni, other righteous occupations with a cause by which one can perform what is to be done for deities, without committing evil deeds, and by following a path of merit.
What do you think, Dhanañjāni: would it be better for someone to act unrighteously and unjustly for the sake of a king, or for someone to act righteously and justly for the sake of a king?”
“Indeed, Master Sāriputta, if one were to act unrighteously and improperly for the sake of a king, that would not be better;
but if, Master Sāriputta, one were to act righteously and properly for the sake of a king, that alone would be better here.
For, Master Sāriputta, acting righteously and properly is better than acting unrighteously and improperly.”
“There are, Dhanañjāni, other lawful occupations that have a cause, by which one can perform the king’s royal duties, commit no evil deed, and practice the way of merit.

What do you think, Dhanañjāni: would it be better for one who, for the sake of nourishing and increasing the body, were to live unrighteously and immorally, or for one who, for the sake of nourishing and increasing the body, were to live righteously and morally?”
“Master Sāriputta, for one who would practice unrighteousness and act unfairly for the sake of nourishing and strengthening the body, that is not better.
But for one who would practice righteousness and act fairly for the sake of nourishing and strengthening the body, that alone is better here.
Master Sāriputta, righteous conduct and fair conduct are better than unrighteous conduct and unfair conduct.”
“Dhanañjāni, there are indeed other righteous occupations with their own causes, by which one can satisfy and nourish the body, without committing evil deeds and while practicing the path of merit.
Then the brahmin Dhanañjāni, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Venerable Sāriputta’s words, rose from his seat and departed.
Later on, the brahmin Dhanañjāni became afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
Then the brahmin Dhanañjāni addressed a certain man:
“Come, good man, go to where the Blessed One is; having approached him, pay homage with your head at the Blessed One’s feet in my name, saying:
‘Venerable sir, the brahmin Dhanañjāni is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.’”
"Thus he pays homage at the Blessed One’s feet with his head.
Then approach the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, pay homage at the Venerable Sāriputta’s feet with your head in my name, saying:
"Venerable sir, the brahmin Dhanañjāni is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill."
“Thus he pays homage at the feet of the Venerable Sāriputta with his head.
And speak thus:
‘It would be well, venerable sir, if the Venerable Sāriputta would visit the residence of the brahmin Dhanañjāni out of compassion.’”
“Yes, venerable sir,” that man replied to the brahmin Dhanañjāni.
He approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the man said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the brahmin Dhanañjāni is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
He pays homage with his head at the Blessed One’s feet.
Then he approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Sāriputta, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, that man said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Venerable sir, the brahmin Dhanañjāni is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
He pays homage with his head at the feet of the Venerable Sāriputta and says this:
‘It would be well, venerable sir, if the Venerable Sāriputta would visit the residence of the brahmin Dhanañjāni out of compassion.’”
The Venerable Sāriputta consented by remaining silent.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, went to the residence of the brahmin Dhanañjāni;
having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Venerable...
Sāriputta said this to the brahmin Dhanañjāni:
“I hope you are bearing up, Dhanañjāni; I hope you are getting by. I hope that your painful feelings are subsiding and not increasing, and that their subsiding is apparent, not their increase?
“Master Sāriputta, I am not bearing up, nor am I getting by. My painful feelings are severe; they are increasing and not subsiding. Their increase is apparent, not their subsiding.”
"Just as, Master Sāriputta, a strong man might strike one on the head with a sharp spear, even so, Master Sāriputta, violent winds are piercing my head.
It is neither bearable nor sustainable for me, Master Sāriputta. My intense painful feelings are increasing, not subsiding; their increase is apparent, not their subsiding."
"Just as if, Master Sāriputta, a strong man were to bind a firm leather thong around my head as a headband, even so, Master Sāriputta, there is an intense pain in my head.
It is not bearable for me, Master Sāriputta, nor can I endure it. My sharp painful feelings are increasing, not subsiding; their increase is apparent, not their subsiding."
"Just as, Master Sāriputta, a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice might cut open a belly with a sharp butcher’s knife, even so, Master Sāriputta, violent winds cut through my belly.
It is not bearable for me, Master Sāriputta, it is not sustainable. My intense painful feelings are increasing, not subsiding; their increase is apparent, not their subsiding."

“Just as if, Master Sāriputta, two strong men were to seize a weaker man by both arms and roast him over a pit of glowing embers, scorching him thoroughly; even so, Master Sāriputta, there is an excessive burning in my body.
It is neither bearable nor sustainable for me, Master Sāriputta. My sharp painful feelings are increasing, not subsiding. Their increase is apparent, not their subsiding.”
“What do you think, Dhanañjāni, which is better:
hell or the animal realm?
“The animal realm, Master Sāriputta, is better than hell.”
“What do you think, Dhanañjāni, which is better:
the animal realm or the sphere of hungry ghosts?
“The sphere of hungry ghosts is better than the animal realm, Master Sāriputta.”
“What do you think, Dhanañjāni, which is better—
the realm of the hungry ghosts or human beings?
“Human beings, Master Sāriputta, are better than the realm of the hungry ghosts.”
“What do you think, Dhanañjāni, which is better:
human beings or the gods of the Four Great Kings?
“The gods of the Four Great Kings, Master Sāriputta, are better than human beings.”
“What do you think, Dhanañjāni, which is better:
the gods of the Four Great Kings or the gods of the Thirty-three?
“The gods of the Thirty-three, Master Sāriputta, are better than the gods of the Four Great Kings.”
“What do you think, Dhanañjāni, which is better:
the Tāvatiṃsa devas or the Yāma devas?
“The Yāma devas, Master Sāriputta, are better than the Tāvatiṃsa devas.”
“What do you think, Dhanañjāni, which is better:
the Yāma devas or the Tusita devas?
“The Tusita devas, Master Sāriputta, are better than the Yāma devas.”
“What do you think, Dhanañjāni, which is better:
the Tusita gods or the gods who delight in creation?
“The gods who delight in creation, Master Sāriputta, are better than the Tusita gods.”
“What do you think, Dhanañjāni, which is better:
the gods who delight in creation or the gods who wield power over the creations of others?
“The gods who wield power over the creations of others, Master Sāriputta, are better than the gods who delight in creation.”
“What do you think, Dhanañjāni, which is better:
the gods who wield power over the creations of others, or the Brahmā world?
“The Brahmā world,” said the venerable Sāriputta.
‘The Brahmā-world,’ Venerable Sāriputta has said.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“These brahmins are indeed intent upon the Brahmā-world.”
"What if I were to teach the path to the company of Brahmā to the brahmin Dhanañjāni?
"Dhanañjāni, I shall teach you the path to the company of Brahmā;
listen to it and attend closely, and I will speak."
“Yes, sir,” the brahmin Dhanañjāni replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
“And what, Dhanañjāni, is the path to the company of Brahmā?”
"Here, Dhanañjāni, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness,
likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself,
he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness— vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity."
He dwells pervading [the world] with a mind imbued with non-ill will.
This, Dhanañjāni, is the path to the company of the Brahmās.
Furthermore, Dhanañjāni, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind imbued with compassion …pe… [as before].
With a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy...
with a mind accompanied by equanimity, he dwells pervading one direction, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth;
thus above, below, across, everywhere, in all respects, the entire world, with a mind accompanied by equanimity.
“He dwells having pervaded with a mind that is vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
This, Dhanañjāni, is the path to the company of the Brahmās.
“In that case, Master Sāriputta, please pay homage with your head at the Blessed One’s feet in my name, saying:”
“Venerable sir, the brahmin Dhanañjāni is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
He pays homage with his head at the Blessed One’s feet.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta, having established the brahmin Dhanañjāni in the inferior Brahmā world—since there was still more to be done—rose from his seat and departed.
Then, not long after the Venerable Sāriputta had departed, the brahmin Dhanañjāni passed away and was reborn in the Brahmā world.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, this Sāriputta, having established the brahmin Dhanañjāni—who still had much more to be done—in the lower Brahmā world, rose from his seat and departed."

Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the brahmin Dhanañjāni is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill;
he pays homage at the feet of the Blessed One with his head.”
“But, Sāriputta, why did you get up from your seat and depart while there was still more to be done, after having established the brahmin Dhanañjāni in the inferior Brahmā world?
“Venerable sir, it occurred to me:
‘These brahmins are intent upon the Brahmā world; what if I were to teach the brahmin Dhanañjāni the path to the companionship of Brahmā?’”
“Sāriputta, the brahmin Dhanañjāni has passed away and has been reborn in the Brahmā world.
The seventh sutta, the Dhanañjānisutta, is finished.
